name: Street Custom 'Glass Garden' Caltrops
description: Improvised caltrops fabricated from broken glass, bent nails, or 3D-printed polymer spikes designed to puncture footwear and vehicle tires. Glass Garden caltrops are scattered in pursuit paths, around defensive positions, or across roadways as area denial tools. The most common variant uses heat-bent roofing nails welded at angles so that one point always faces upward regardless of how the device lands. More sophisticated versions include hollow spikes containing irritant compounds that release into the puncture wound. The name comes from the practice of scattering them across an area like seeds — from above, a deployed field of caltrops on dark pavement is invisible until you step on one.
specifications:
construction: Bent nails, broken glass, or 3D-printed polymer
spike height: 2-4 cm
deployment density: 20-50 per square meter for effective coverage
weight: 2-5 grams each
packaging: Typically carried in cloth bags of 100-500
cost per unit: Φ0.10-0.50 depending on construction
effective against: Foot traffic, standard vehicle tires, thin-soled footwear
story_hooks: A major transit route has been seeded with thousands of caltrops embedded with a slow-acting corrosive — vehicles that drive over them experience tire failure hours later, far from the deployment site.
Someone is deploying caltrops around the perimeter of a Tier 1 medical clinic every night, preventing patients from reaching the entrance — the clinic is treating people the deployer wants dead.

physical_description.visual_profile: A malicious four-pointed star or irregular spike cluster, deliberately designed so one point always faces upward. Resembles a medieval caltrop rendered in scrap materials—aggressive, primitive, lethal in its simplicity.
physical_description.dimensions: Spike height: 2-4 cm. Base footprint varies by construction; nail variants roughly 3-5 cm across, polymer versions slightly more uniform at 4-6 cm diameter.
physical_description.weight_description: Deceptively light—2-5 grams per unit. Feels negligible in a handful, which makes bulk deployment feasible. A cloth bag of 100-500 feels substantial but portable, like carrying ball bearings.
physical_description.primary_material: Mixed construction variants: heat-bent mild steel roofing nails, jagged glass shards fused or glued to polymer bases, or 3D-printed rigid polymer spikes with sharp edges.
physical_description.finish: Dull, oxidized steel on nail variants; milky or translucent on glass versions with rough, hazardous fracture lines; matte grey or industrial tan on polymer prints. No protective coating—intentionally exposed and abrasive.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal grey and rust-brown for steel; clear to amber for glass with visible fracture webs; grey or tan for polymer with occasional streaks of old blood or dirt.
physical_description.grip_texture: Not designed for grip—the spikes themselves are rough and sharp. Transported in cloth bags that feel coarse and worn. Handling requires gloves or careful pinching at the base.
distinctive_features: Four or more sharpened points radiating from center—one always faces upward on landing
Visible welds or solder joints on metal variants, rough and industrial
Hollow polymer spike variants with small apertures for irritant compound dispersal
Dried residue or discoloration indicating use or chemical loading
Irregular edges and micro-fractures catching light unpredictably
Faint tool marks and signs of improvised fabrication
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: None—'Street Custom' is anonymous fabrication. Occasional street crew tags or ownership marks scratched into polymer variants, but these are incidental, not branding.
physical_description.condition_typical: Battle-worn and functional. Spikes show signs of repeated handling, minor dulling from contact with pavement, possible bloodstains, scattered dirt, and oxidation. Polymer variants may be slightly warped from heat. Glass versions have micro-chips and visible stress fractures.
